lesson_scope: Work done by a constant force acting in the direction of motion, at an angle to horizontal motion, and along or at an angle to an inclined plane; calculation of normal contact force and work done against friction; work done against gravity on inclines; power and work relationships at constant speed.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Horizontal pulling force parallel to motion

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Horizontal pulling force parallel to motion

hints: Use the work done formula for a force acting in the direction of motion: $W = Fd$.
Substitute $F = 85\text{ N}$ and $d = 16\text{ m}$ to calculate $W = 85 \times 16 = 1360\text{ J}$.

walkthrough.text:
State the governing formula for work done by a constant force in the direction of motion:
$$W = Fd$$
Here the tension $F = 85\text{ N}$ acts parallel to the displacement $d = 16\text{ m}$.

Calculate the numerical value of the work done:
$$W = 85 \times 16 = 1360\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Identify the applied force and the displacement:
- The tension acts horizontally along the floor:
$$F = 85\text{ N},\quad d = 16\text{ m}$$
Because force and displacement point in the exact same direction, the angle is $\theta = 0^\circ$.

Compute the energy transferred by the cable:
- Multiply force by distance directly:
$$W = 85 \times 16 = 1360\text{ J}$$
The cable does $1360\text{ J}$ of work on the crate.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $W = Fd$ with $F = 85$ and $d = 16$.
Obtains work done $W = 1360\text{ J}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 2: Pulling force inclined above the horizontal

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 2: Pulling force inclined above the horizontal

hints: Only the component of force in the direction of motion does work: $W = Fd\cos\theta$.
Substitute $F = 60\text{ N}$, $d = 25\text{ m}$, and $\theta = 35^\circ$ to evaluate $60 \times 25 \times \cos 35^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve the tension force in the direction of displacement along the horizontal:
$$F_x = F\cos\theta = 60\cos 35^\circ\text{ N}$$
The work done over displacement $d = 25\text{ m}$ is:
$$W = (F\cos\theta)d = (60\cos 35^\circ)(25)$$

Evaluate the product to 3 significant figures:
$$W = 1500\cos 35^\circ \approx 1228.7\text{ J} \approx 1230\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find the effective component of the pulling force:
- Only the horizontal component moves the sledge forward:
$$F_x = 60\cos 35^\circ \approx 49.15\text{ N}$$
The vertical component reduces normal contact force, but does zero work because there is no vertical motion.

Multiply effective force by displacement:
- Over a distance of $25\text{ m}$:
$$W = 49.149 \times 25 \approx 1230\text{ J}$$
The rope does $1230\text{ J}$ of work on the sledge.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $W = Fd\cos\theta$ with $F = 60$, $d = 25$, and $\theta = 35^\circ$.
Obtains work done $W = 1230\text{ J}$ (or $1229\text{ J}$).

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 4: Calculating inclination angle from work done and displacement

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 4: Calculating inclination angle from work done and displacement

hints: Equate the given work done to the formula $W = Fd\cos\theta$.
Solve $\cos\theta = \frac{420}{45 \times 14} = \frac{420}{630} = \frac{2}{3}$ using the inverse cosine function.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute the given values into the work done relation:
$$W = Fd\cos\theta$$
$$420 = 45 \times 14 \times \cos\theta = 630\cos\theta$$

Solve for $\cos\theta$ and determine the angle $\theta$:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{420}{630} = \frac{2}{3}$$
$$\theta = \arccos\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \approx 48.1897^\circ \approx 48.2^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Set up the work equation:
- The tension does $420\text{ J}$ of work over $14\text{ m}$:
$$420 = 45 \times 14 \times \cos\theta$$
- Multiplying force and distance gives:
$$630\cos\theta = 420$$

Isolate and evaluate the angle:
- Find the cosine of the angle:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{420}{630} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.6667$$
- Apply inverse cosine:
$$\theta = \arccos(0.6667) \approx 48.2^\circ$$
The rope is pulled at an angle of $48.2^\circ$ to the horizontal.

ai_rubric.observable: Sets up $420 = 45 \times 14 \times \cos\theta$ and solves for $\cos\theta$.
Obtains $\theta = 48.2^\circ$ (or $48.19^\circ$).

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 5: Work done by pulling force parallel to incline and by normal reaction

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 5: Work done by pulling force parallel to incline and by normal reaction

hints: The tension acts in the exact direction of motion along the slope, so $W = Fd$.
The normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope, so the angle between force and displacement is $90^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the work done by the tension pulling parallel to the plane:
$$W_{\text{tension}} = Fd\cos 0^\circ = 50 \times 12 = 600\text{ J}$$

Evaluate the work done by the normal contact force:
$$W_{\text{normal}} = Rd\cos 90^\circ = 0\text{ J}$$
Because the normal contact force is perpendicular to the displacement at every point, it does zero work.

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Compute the work done by the rope:
- The rope pulls directly along the surface of the slope:
$$W_{\text{tension}} = 50 \times 12 = 600\text{ J}$$
All $50\text{ N}$ acts along the motion.

Examine the normal reaction force:
- The slope pushes perpendicular to the motion at an angle of $90^\circ$:
$$\cos 90^\circ = 0 \implies W_{\text{normal}} = 0\text{ J}$$
A contact force perpendicular to motion does zero work.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates work done by tension as $W = 50 \times 12 = 600\text{ J}$.
States that work done by the normal contact force is $0\text{ J}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 1: Horizontal motion at constant speed under inclined tension and resistance

hints: When a body moves at constant speed, the net horizontal force is zero, so resistance equals the horizontal component of tension.
The work done against resistance is the resistance force multiplied by distance, which equals the work done by the tension.

walkthrough.text:
Apply Newton's first law for constant horizontal speed ($a = 0$):
$$\Sigma F_x = 0 \implies T\cos 25^\circ - R_{\text{resist}} = 0$$
$$R_{\text{resist}} = 80\cos 25^\circ \approx 72.505\text{ N} \approx 72.5\text{ N}$$

Calculate the work done against the resisting force:
$$W_{\text{resist}} = R_{\text{resist}} \times d = (80\cos 25^\circ)(16) = 1280\cos 25^\circ \approx 1160\text{ J}$$
Because speed is constant, the work done by the pulling tension exactly equals the work done against resistance.

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Determine the resistance force:
- Zero acceleration means horizontal forces are balanced:
$$R_{\text{resist}} = 80\cos 25^\circ \approx 72.5\text{ N}$$
The resistance matches the forward pulling component exactly.

Determine work against resistance:
- Multiply the resisting force by the distance:
$$W_{\text{resist}} = 72.505 \times 16 \approx 1160\text{ J}$$
All $1160\text{ J}$ provided by the tension is dissipated overcoming resistance.

ai_rubric.observable: States that resisting force equals horizontal component of tension: $R_{\text{resist}} = 80\cos 25^\circ \approx 72.5\text{ N}$.
States work done against resistance is $W_{\text{resist}} = 72.5 \times 16 \approx 1160\text{ J}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 2: Rough horizontal surface with friction and inclined pulling force

hints: Resolve forces vertically: normal reaction plus the vertical component of the pulling force balances weight.
Calculate $R = 200 - 70\sin 30^\circ = 165\text{ N}$, then apply $F_r = \mu R$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces vertically in equilibrium:
$$R + P\sin 30^\circ = mg$$
$$R + 70(0.5) = 20(10) = 200$$
$$R = 200 - 35 = 165\text{ N}$$

Calculate the limiting frictional force using $F_r = \mu R$:
$$F_r = 0.25 \times 165 = 41.25\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Balance the vertical forces:
- The pulling force lifts the block slightly with upward component $70\sin 30^\circ = 35\text{ N}$:
$$R = mg - 35 = 200 - 35 = 165\text{ N}$$
The normal reaction is reduced from $200\text{ N}$ to $165\text{ N}$.

Compute the frictional force:
- Friction depends on this reduced normal contact force:
$$F_r = \mu R = 0.25 \times 165 = 41.25\text{ N}$$
This confirms the frictional force is exactly $41.25\text{ N}$ opposing motion.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves vertically to form $R + 70\sin 30^\circ = 20(10)$ and finds $R = 165\text{ N}$.
Calculates $F_r = \mu R = 0.25 \times 165 = 41.25\text{ N}$ correctly.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 2: Rough horizontal surface with friction and inclined pulling force

hints: The work done by $P$ is $(P\cos 30^\circ) \times d$, taking only the component parallel to the surface.
The work done against friction is the friction force multiplied by distance: $41.25 \times 8 = 330\text{ J}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the work done by the pulling force $P$ along the horizontal displacement $d = 8\text{ m}$:
$$W_P = (P\cos\theta)d = (70\cos 30^\circ)(8) = 560\cos 30^\circ$$
$$W_P = 560 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 280\sqrt{3} \approx 484.97\text{ J} \approx 485\text{ J}$$

Calculate the work done against friction over the $8\text{ m}$ displacement:
$$W_{\text{fric}} = F_r \times d = 41.25 \times 8 = 330\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Compute work supplied by the pulling force:
- Only the horizontal component of $P$ does work:
$$W_P = (70\cos 30^\circ) \times 8 = 560\cos 30^\circ \approx 485\text{ J}$$
The pulling force injects $485\text{ J}$ of energy into the system.

Compute work lost to friction:
- Friction acts continuously opposing the $8\text{ m}$ slide:
$$W_{\text{fric}} = 41.25 \times 8 = 330\text{ J}$$
Out of the $485\text{ J}$ supplied, $330\text{ J}$ is dissipated as thermal energy against friction.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $W_P = (70\cos 30^\circ) \times 8$ for the work done by the pulling force.
Obtains work done by pulling force $W_P = 485\text{ J}$ (or $484.97\dots\text{ J}$).
Calculates work done against friction as $W_{\text{fric}} = 41.25 \times 8 = 330\text{ J}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 1: Simultaneous determination of pulling angle and tension from work and friction equilibrium

hints: Constant speed means distance is simply $d = vt = 2 \times 15 = 30\text{ m}$.
Relate work done to the horizontal component of tension: $W = (T\cos\theta)d$.
Substitute $W = 2400\text{ J}$ and $d = 30\text{ m}$ into $2400 = (T\cos\theta)(30)$ to solve for $T\cos\theta$.
Evaluating the division gives the exact horizontal tension component: $T\cos\theta = 80\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the distance travelled at constant speed:
$$d = vt = 2 \times 15 = 30\text{ m}$$

Express work done in terms of the horizontal component of tension:
$$W = (T\cos\theta)d$$
$$2400 = (T\cos\theta)(30) \implies T\cos\theta = \frac{2400}{30} = 80\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find displacement from steady velocity:
- The container moves at $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ across $15\text{ s}$:
$$d = 2 \times 15 = 30\text{ m}$$

Extract the horizontal pulling force component:
- Total work done is force component times displacement:
$$2400 = T\cos\theta \times 30 \implies T\cos\theta = 80\text{ N}$$
The horizontal component pulling the container is exactly $80\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 1: Simultaneous determination of pulling angle and tension from work and friction equilibrium

hints: At constant speed, acceleration is zero, so $T\cos\theta = F_r = \mu R$.
Resolve vertically: $R + T\sin\theta = mg = 500 \implies R = 500 - T\sin\theta$.
Substitute $R$ into the horizontal equation: $80 = 0.2(500 - T\sin\theta) = 100 - 0.2T\sin\theta$.
Solve for the vertical component: $0.2T\sin\theta = 20 \implies T\sin\theta = 100\text{ N}$.
Use $\tan\theta = \frac{T\sin\theta}{T\cos\theta} = \frac{100}{80} = 1.25$ to find $\theta$, then find $T$ using Pythagoras or $T = \frac{80}{\cos\theta}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the ground to express the normal contact force:
$$R + T\sin\theta = mg = (50)(10) = 500$$
$$R = 500 - T\sin\theta\text{ N}$$

Apply the horizontal equilibrium condition for constant velocity ($a = 0$):
$$T\cos\theta = F_r = \mu R$$
$$80 = 0.2(500 - T\sin\theta) = 100 - 0.2T\sin\theta$$
$$0.2T\sin\theta = 20 \implies T\sin\theta = 100\text{ N}$$

Determine the angle $\theta$ from the ratio of vertical and horizontal components:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{T\sin\theta}{T\cos\theta} = \frac{100}{80} = 1.25$$
$$\theta = \arctan(1.25) \approx 51.340^\circ \approx 51.3^\circ$$

Calculate the magnitude of the tension $T$:
$$T = \sqrt{(T\cos\theta)^2 + (T\sin\theta)^2} = \sqrt{80^2 + 100^2} = \sqrt{6400 + 10000} = \sqrt{16400}$$
$$T \approx 128.06\text{ N} \approx 128\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Formulate normal contact force:
- Upward pull reduces the load pressed onto the dock:
$$R = mg - T\sin\theta = 500 - T\sin\theta$$

Equate horizontal driving force to friction:
- Because speed is constant, driving force balances friction:
$$80 = 0.2(500 - T\sin\theta) = 100 - 0.2T\sin\theta$$
- Solving for vertical component:
$$0.2T\sin\theta = 20 \implies T\sin\theta = 100\text{ N}$$

Find the angle of inclination:
- Divide the two component equations:
$$\tan\theta = \frac{100}{80} = 1.25 \implies \theta = \arctan(1.25) \approx 51.3^\circ$$
The rope pulls at $51.3^\circ$ to the horizontal.

Calculate total tension magnitude:
- Recombine orthogonal components using Pythagoras:
$$T = \sqrt{80^2 + 100^2} = \sqrt{16400} \approx 128\text{ N}$$
The required pulling tension is $128\text{ N}$.
